questions.subject: Maths
questions.series: Original AQA Year 1 Pure targeted application
questions.question: Reconstruct and interpret an exponential model from a natural-log graph
questions.subtopic: Reconstruct and interpret an exponential model from a natural-log graph
questions.prompt: A quantity P is modelled by P=Ae^(−kt), where A>0 and k>0. A straight-line graph of ln P against t passes through (2, 1.5) and (7, 0.5). (a) Find k and ln A. (b) Write an exact expression for P in terms of t and give A to 3 significant figures. (c) Find the time when P=3, giving your answer to 3 decimal places. (d) Calculate the time for the model quantity to halve, and explain one limitation of using the graph to predict P at t=20. [8 marks]
markPoints: Uses ln P=ln A−kt, identifying −k as gradient and ln A as vertical intercept.
Finds the gradient (0.5−1.5)/(7−2)=−0.2, hence k=0.2.
Uses 1.5=ln A−0.2×2 to obtain ln A=1.9.
States P=e^(1.9−0.2t), equivalently P=e^1.9 e^(−0.2t).
Evaluates A=e^1.9≈6.69 (3 significant figures).
Solves ln 3=1.9−0.2t to obtain t=(1.9−ln 3)/0.2≈4.007.
Finds the halving time ln 2/0.2≈3.466 time units from P(t+h)=P(t)/2.
Explains that t=20 lies outside the plotted data interval 2≤t≤7, so extending the exponential model that far is an unverified extrapolation.
questions.modelAnswer: Taking natural logarithms: ln P=ln A−kt. From the two points, gradient (0.5−1.5)/5=−0.2, so k=0.2. At t=2, 1.5=ln A−0.4 and ln A=1.9. Therefore P=e^(1.9−0.2t), with A=e^1.9≈6.69. When P=3, ln3=1.9−0.2t, so t=(1.9−ln3)/0.2≈4.007. If P(t+h)=P(t)/2, e^(−0.2h)=1/2, so h=ln2/0.2≈3.466 time units. t=20 is outside the available t=2 to 7 observations; the pattern might not continue beyond the observations.
questions.questionType: manually reviewed multi-step Pure Maths working
questions.manualReviewReason: Do not award credit for a final value without the corresponding log-linear and algebraic working. Exponential parameters and extrapolation interpretation must be checked separately.

questions.question: Find both triangles in an ambiguous sine-rule problem
questions.subtopic: Find both triangles in an ambiguous sine-rule problem
questions.prompt: In triangle ABC, sides a and b are opposite angles A and B respectively. A=30°, a=10 cm and b=14 cm. (a) Use the sine rule to find sin B. (b) Show that two different values of B are possible and calculate both. (c) For each triangle, calculate C and the opposite side c to 3 significant figures. (d) Explain why using only the inverse sine calculator output would miss a valid triangle. [8 marks]
markPoints: Applies a/sin A=b/sin B or equivalently sin B=b sin A/a.
Calculates sin B=(14×sin30°)/10=0.7.
Finds the acute solution B₁=sin⁻¹(0.7)≈44.427°.
Finds the obtuse solution B₂=180°−B₁≈135.573°.
Checks that both values are valid with A=30° and finds C₁≈105.573°.
Finds the second angle C₂≈14.427°.
Applies c/sin C=10/sin30° to get c₁≈19.3 cm and c₂≈4.98 cm (three significant figures).
Explains that sin θ=sin(180°−θ), so the inverse sine principal value does not capture the supplementary-angle case.
questions.modelAnswer: The sine rule gives sinB=(14 sin30°)/10=0.7. Hence B₁=sin⁻¹(0.7)≈44.427° or B₂=180°−44.427°≈135.573°. Both satisfy A+B<180°. For B₁, C₁=180−30−44.427≈105.573° and c₁=(10/sin30°)sin105.573°≈19.3 cm. For B₂, C₂≈14.427° and c₂=(10/sin30°)sin14.427°≈4.98 cm. The supplementary angle gives the same sine value, so taking only sin⁻¹(0.7) misses the second valid triangle.
questions.questionType: manually reviewed multi-step Pure Maths working
questions.manualReviewReason: Inspect both angle branches, triangle validity and both side lengths. A single inverse-sine answer cannot receive the second-triangle marks.

questions.question: Maximise the volume of an open-top box using differentiation
questions.subtopic: Maximise the volume of an open-top box using differentiation
questions.prompt: A 20 cm by 12 cm rectangle of card has a square of side x cm cut from each corner. The edges are folded up to form an open-top box. (a) Show that its volume is V=4x³−64x²+240x, stating the possible values of x. (b) Find every stationary value of x and decide which is physically possible. (c) Find the maximum box volume to 3 significant figures, and justify that it is a maximum. [7 marks]
markPoints: Uses dimensions (20−2x), (12−2x) and height x, so V=x(20−2x)(12−2x).
Expands V=4x³−64x²+240x and gives the physical domain 0<x<6.
Differentiates correctly: dV/dx=12x²−128x+240.
Solves dV/dx=0 to obtain x=(16±2√19)/3 (or numerically equivalent).
Rejects the larger root because it exceeds the physical domain and retains x≈2.427 cm.
Substitutes to obtain Vmax≈263 cm³ to 3 significant figures.
Justifies maximum using d²V/dx²=24x−128<0 at x≈2.427, or a valid derivative-sign argument.
questions.modelAnswer: The volume is V=x(20−2x)(12−2x)=4x³−64x²+240x. To keep both base lengths positive, 0<x<6. Differentiate: dV/dx=12x²−128x+240=4(3x²−32x+60). Solving 3x²−32x+60=0 gives x=(16±2√19)/3. The larger value ≈8.239 cm is impossible; the smaller ≈2.427 cm is feasible. Substitution into V=x(20−2x)(12−2x) gives approximately 263 cm³ (3 significant figures). At x≈2.427, d²V/dx²=24x−128<0, so the stationary value is a maximum.
questions.questionType: manually reviewed multi-step Pure Maths working
questions.manualReviewReason: Require geometric modelling, the physical domain, differentiation, sensible-root selection and a valid maximum argument; these are marks for working, not isolated keywords.
